scope: Current catalogue scan across names, tracks, descriptions, profiles, topics and methods. Compared candidate contributions against required physical theory, chemical theory and laboratory sequence.
lifeEnvironmentCandidate: Reassessed without retaining the superseded schedule. Dynamic Earth supports geophysical processes; Environmental Biogeochemistry supports applied aqueous, mineral and redox chemistry; Sustainability Essentials introduces physical principles. Even assuming every old selection could be scheduled, that combination lacks upper-level mechanics, electromagnetism, quantum theory, chemical bonding, synthesis and instrumental analysis. Moving Research in a Sustainable Delta to its only current offering would bring a team research project into the opening term and would not address the academic gaps.
biomedicalCandidate: The repaired illustrative schedule places Image Processing and Computer Vision in 2027h1 and Introduction to Data Science in 2027h2. Biochemistry, molecular cell biology and the laboratory provide strong life-science overlap; imaging and linear systems teach image and signal methods, with no corresponding optics and electromagnetic theory sequence. Biomedical breadth and evidence synthesis cannot close the chemistry gaps.
materialsCandidate: The sustainability gateway and delta innovation course contribute material choice and sustainability design; adding them to the science and mathematics content above still lacks the required advanced theoretical and experimental physical chemistry progression.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
ACCPPDE101.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
ACCPPDE101.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
ACCPPDE101.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

BENGATE102.name: Research Methods & Statistics
BENGATE102.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
BENGATE102.profile: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.
BENGATE102.topics: Scientific inquiry and hypotheses; Operationalization and measurement; Reliability and validity; Survey construction and sampling; Randomized and quasi-experimental designs; Nonexperimental and qualitative research; Descriptive statistics; Sampling distributions and estimation; Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals; Association and regression; Research ethics and anonymous data collection
BENGATE102.methods: Survey design; Probability and nonprobability sampling; Experimental and nonexperimental research design; R and R Commander data analysis; Descriptive statistics and visualization; Scale-reliability analysis; One- and two-sample mean tests; ANOVA; Chi-square tests; Correlation and regression; Empirical data collection and analysis

DISDATA111.name: Introduction to Data Science
DISDATA111.description2: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
DISDATA111.profile: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.
DISDATA111.topics: Data visualization; Exploratory data analysis; Tidy data; Data transformation and integration; Dates and times; Web data; Text data; Geospatial data; Programming functions; Data-based research questions
DISDATA111.methods: R programming; ggplot visualization and grammar of graphics; Data cleaning, tidying and transformation; Data import and joins; Web scraping; Text-data analysis; Geospatial-data analysis

DISDATA211.name: Machine Learning
DISDATA211.description2: Covers core machine learning techniques from linear regression to advanced tree‑based methods. Discusses strengths and weaknesses and applies methods to real data from fields like medicine, physics and economics.
DISDATA211.profile: Introduces statistical learning for understanding data and predicting outcomes. Students study regression and classification, model accuracy, resampling, regularization, nonlinear models, trees, support vector machines and unsupervised learning. Practical assignments evaluate methods on real data using R or Python. Projects emphasize informative predictor construction, test-set prediction, appropriate model choice and clear reporting of results and limitations.
DISDATA211.topics: Prediction and model accuracy; Regression and classification; Resampling and validation; Model selection and regularization; High-dimensional data; Nonlinear regression; Tree-based learning; Support vector methods; Dimension reduction; Unsupervised learning; Feature engineering
DISDATA211.methods: Linear and logistic regression; Generative classification; Cross-validation and bootstrap; Subset selection; Ridge regression and LASSO; Splines and generalized additive models; Basic and advanced decision-tree methods; Support vector machines; Principal component analysis; Clustering; Predictive-performance evaluation; R or Python implementation

DISDATA212.name: Image Processing & Computer Vision
DISDATA212.description2: Covers processing and analysis of image data, including feature detection and tracking. Discusses applications in medicine, self‑driving vehicles, gaming, robotics and traffic management.
DISDATA212.profile: Examines how digital images are represented, processed and interpreted to recognize structures and objects. Spatial and spectral representations, colour and image statistics support filtering, segmentation, curve and feature detection, tracking and object classification. Students use Python and OpenCV to implement image-processing techniques, investigate spectral representations, and build a recognition pipeline whose performance is benchmarked on previously unseen images.
DISDATA212.topics: Spatial and spectral image representations; Cameras and calibration; Colour models and quantization; Image histograms; Point operators; Linear and nonlinear filters; Edges and contours; Mathematical morphology; Image segmentation; Curve and corner detection; Feature detection and tracking; Object localization and classification; Recognition performance
DISDATA212.methods: Python and OpenCV programming; Image filtering; Histogram and point transformations; Morphological image processing; Hough transform; Image segmentation; Feature matching and tracking; Recognition-pipeline design; Benchmark evaluation on unseen images

DISDATA311.name: Neural Networks & Deep Learning
DISDATA311.description2: Explores theory and practice of neural networks. Students build basic networks and progress to complex networks for computer vision, and discuss recent developments in large language and image generation models.
DISDATA311.profile: Develops neural-network theory and practical implementation in Python, Keras and TensorFlow. Students build and train simple networks before studying multilayer architectures, backpropagation, regularization and model evaluation. Later work applies deep learning to computer vision, time series and text, including transformers. Projects construct predictors for tabular data and investigate an independently chosen image- or text-based prediction problem, with experimental results reported in a paper.
DISDATA311.topics: Perceptrons and ADALINE; Multilayer neural networks; Gradient descent and backpropagation; Bias-variance trade-off and regularization; Computation graphs; Network architectures and interpretation; Computer vision; Time-series learning; Text classification and generation; Transformers and large language models; Feature engineering; Predictive performance
DISDATA311.methods: Python programming; Keras and TensorFlow network implementation; Gradient-descent training; Backpropagation implementation; Neural-network performance evaluation; Tabular prediction; Image classification; Text classification and generation; Deep-learning experimental design

DISGATE101.name: Introduction to Programming
DISGATE101.description2: Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and develops computational problem‑solving skills.
DISGATE101.profile: Introduces computational problem-solving and programming in Python. Students develop structured programs using branching, iteration, functions and data collections, then progress to recursion, exception handling and object-oriented programming with inheritance. Elements of logic, sets and enumeration support computational reasoning. Exercises and projects require students to write, trace, test, debug and explain programs that solve problems of moderate complexity.
DISGATE101.topics: Python language fundamentals; Strings and input/output; Branching and loops; Functions; Tuples, lists, sets and dictionaries; Aliasing and cloning; Recursion; Exceptions and assertions; Object-oriented programming; Inheritance; Computational problem-solving
DISGATE101.methods: Structured programming in Python; Object-oriented programming; Recursive problem-solving; Program tracing; Testing and debugging; Exception handling

DISGATE102.name: Mathematical Methods
DISGATE102.description2: Introduces linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) and calculus (limits, differentiation, integration) to construct and solve equations. Provides problem‑solving skills applicable across disciplines.
DISGATE102.profile: Develops single-variable calculus and related mathematical tools for modelling scientific problems. Functions, limits and differentiation lead to optimization, Taylor series, complex numbers, integration and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica, including numerical approximation. A project implements, analyzes and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and explanation of the computational results.
DISGATE102.topics: Functions and limits; Continuity; Differentiation; Optimization; Taylor series; Complex numbers; Definite and indefinite integrals; Integration techniques; First-order differential equations; Population-growth and predator–prey models; Second-order linear differential equations; Dynamic models
DISGATE102.methods: Analytical differentiation and integration; Taylor approximation; Newton's method; Numerical integration; Euler's method; Analytical solution of differential equations; Computer algebra with Mathematica; Dynamic-model implementation and analysis

DISMATH211.name: Linear Algebra
DISMATH211.description2: Introduces systems of equations, vectors, matrices and linear spaces with emphasis on visual and conceptual understanding. Applies concepts across fields and includes hands‑on exercises using computer algebra software.
DISMATH211.profile: Develops linear algebra from systems of equations and matrix operations to vector spaces, linear transformations, eigenvalues and orthogonality. Students study least-squares approximation, symmetric matrices, quadratic forms and singular value decomposition. Applications include discrete signals, difference equations, Markov chains, dynamical systems, graphics and principal component analysis. Mathematica exercises teach computer-algebra approaches to larger problems alongside analytical problem-solving.
DISMATH211.topics: Linear systems and matrix algebra; Linear independence, span, basis, dimension and rank; Linear transformations; Determinants and invertibility; Vector spaces; Eigenvalues and eigenvectors; Difference equations and Markov chains; Discrete signals and Fourier series; Orthogonality and inner products; Quadratic forms and constrained optimization; Singular value decomposition; Principal component analysis
DISMATH211.methods: Row reduction; Matrix factorization and diagonalization; Change of basis; Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization; Orthogonal projection; Least-squares fitting and QR factorization; Singular value decomposition; Principal component analysis; Mathematica computer-algebra computation

DISMATH213.name: Computational & Numerical Methods
DISMATH213.description2: Introduces numerical methods such as root‑finding, interpolation, numerical differentiation and integration and solving differential equations. Emphasises algorithm accuracy, stability and efficiency and uses computer algebra software.
DISMATH213.profile: Develops numerical solutions to mathematical problems that lack convenient analytical solutions, emphasizing when algorithms work and how to validate their output. Students study numerical root finding, interpolation, differentiation, quadrature, ordinary differential equations, and linear and nonlinear systems. Mathematica notebooks apply and compare textbook algorithms with built-in routines, with attention to roundoff, convergence, error, stability and sensitivity.
DISMATH213.topics: Computer arithmetic and roundoff; Algorithm convergence and error; Scalar root finding; Polynomial interpolation and splines; Parametric curves; Numerical differentiation and integration; Initial-value problems; Multistep and adaptive differential-equation methods; Stability and stiff equations; Linear systems and matrix factorization; Nonlinear systems; Numerical-result validation
DISMATH213.methods: Mathematica numerical computation; Bisection, fixed-point, Newton and secant methods; Polynomial and spline interpolation; Numerical differentiation and Richardson extrapolation; Simpson, Romberg and Gaussian quadrature; Adaptive quadrature; Euler and Runge-Kutta methods; Multistep predictor-corrector methods; Gaussian elimination and pivoting; Matrix factorizations; Newton and quasi-Newton methods for systems; Steepest descent; Continuation methods

DISMATH312.name: Linear Systems
DISMATH312.description2: Focuses on analysis of linear systems from an engineering perspective. Explores representations via differential equations, transfer functions, state‑space and signal‑flow diagrams and discusses applications in control, signal processing and modelling.
DISMATH312.profile: Analyzes continuous- and discrete-time signals and linear time-invariant systems through differential or difference equations, impulse responses and frequency-domain representations. Convolution, Fourier series and transforms lead into sampling and reconstruction, filtering, communication systems, Laplace and Z-transforms, and linear feedback. Mathematica laboratories and an applied project connect mathematical properties to signal processing and system behaviour.
DISMATH312.topics: Continuous- and discrete-time signals; System linearity, causality and stability; Impulse and frequency responses; Convolution; Fourier series and transforms; Time-frequency representations; Sampling, reconstruction and aliasing; Digital filtering; Modulation and multiplexing; Laplace and Z-transforms; Regions of convergence and pole-zero representations; Linear feedback and stability
DISMATH312.methods: Convolution sums and integrals; Fourier-series and Fourier-transform analysis; Bode-plot analysis; Sampling and signal reconstruction; Filter analysis; Modulation and demodulation; Laplace and Z-transform analysis; Block-diagram system analysis; Root-locus analysis; Mathematica signal and system computation

DISMATH314.name: Probability & Statistics
DISMATH314.description2: Provides a foundation in mathematical statistics. Covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; uses computer algebra software to develop theoretical understanding and practical skills.
DISMATH314.profile: Provides a rigorous introduction to probability and mathematical statistics, from probability spaces and random variables to multivariate distributions and statistical inference. Students study estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and maximum-likelihood methods, followed by an introduction to Bayesian reasoning. Mathematica simulations verify analytical results. A substantial project implements and compares random-sampling algorithms, including inverse sampling, accept-reject sampling and Gibbs sampling.
DISMATH314.topics: Probability spaces and conditional probability; Random variables and expectation; Moment-generating functions; Discrete and continuous distributions; Multivariate and conditional distributions; Transformations and correlation; Sampling and order statistics; Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests; Estimation efficiency; Bayesian inference; Monte Carlo methods
DISMATH314.methods: Analytical probability calculation; Maximum-likelihood estimation and testing; Chi-square tests; Bootstrap; EM algorithm; Bayesian updating; Inverse-transform sampling; Accept-reject sampling; Gibbs sampling; Monte Carlo simulation in Mathematica

ENSECOL211.name: The Science of Evolution
ENSECOL211.description2: Evolution is the unifying theory in biology. As such, an understanding of evolutionary biology is vital for understanding the natural world. In this course, we will discuss key concepts in evolution such as population genetics, variation and selection, speciation, macro-evolution and the origins of life. The importance of evolutionary concepts to all other fields of biology will be emphasized, as well as important implications of evolutionary processes in fields like human health and climate change.
ENSECOL211.profile: Examines evolutionary theory from genetic mechanisms to the diversification and history of life. Students study natural selection, variation and drift, population and quantitative genetics, adaptation and sexual reproduction, then species concepts, speciation, phylogeny and macroevolution. Genomics, development, biogeography and coevolution extend the account across scales. A project reconstructs a chosen species' evolutionary history using Tinbergen's four questions.
ENSECOL211.topics: Evidence for evolution; Molecular and Mendelian genetics; Natural selection and genetic drift; Multilocus and quantitative genetics; Adaptation and units of selection; Sexual reproduction; Species concepts and speciation; Phylogeny and classification; Evolutionary biogeography; Evolutionary genomics and development; Coevolution; Evolutionary rates, extinction and radiation
ENSECOL211.methods: Evolutionary-history analysis using Tinbergen's four questions; Phylogenetic reconstruction

ENSECOL212.name: Ecosystems Uncovered: How Nature Works
ENSECOL212.description2: Focuses on basic principles of ecology. Studies how environmental conditions affect organisms and examines ecological principles governing individuals, populations, communities and ecosystems, including ecological modelling and applied case studies.
ENSECOL212.profile: Develops ecological principles from organisms and populations to communities and ecosystems. Environmental conditions, resources and life cycles frame competition, feeding relationships, selection, population dynamics and biodiversity. Energy and matter cycles connect ecological processes to conservation and human impacts. Dedicated practical sessions teach simple ecological modelling in R, and a small research project communicates findings through a poster.
ENSECOL212.topics: Ecology and evolution; Environmental conditions and resources; Climate and life cycles; Ecological niches; Competition and cohabitation; Predation and food webs; Natural selection; Population dynamics; Biodiversity patterns; Ecological succession; Ecosystem energy and matter fluxes; Global cycles; Conservation and human impacts; Ecosystem value
ENSECOL212.methods: Ecological modelling in R; Population-dynamics calculations; Ecosystem energy and matter-flux calculations; Ecological research-project design and analysis

ENSECOL312.name: Sustainable Farming & Innovation
ENSECOL312.description2: Discusses environmental impacts of agriculture and explores sustainable agriculture approaches such as agroecology, organic farming, conservation agriculture, precision agriculture, sustainable livestock farming, agroforestry, permaculture, crop rotation, integrated pest management and sustainable supply chains.
ENSECOL312.profile: Examines how food production can balance human needs with environmental impacts. Students assess current agriculture, horticulture and animal husbandry, their effects on biodiversity and ecosystems, and alternative practices and innovations. Aquaculture, alternative animal-protein sources and farming for other industries extend the comparison. A literature-based project critically investigates a chosen sustainable-farming question and reports the evidence without prescribing a single preferred approach.
ENSECOL312.topics: Agricultural and horticultural systems; Environmental impacts of farming; Wildlife and biodiversity; Modification of current farming practices; Alternative agricultural approaches; Animal husbandry; Aquaculture; Alternative protein sources; Farming for non-food industries; Sustainable-farming innovation
ENSECOL312.methods: Scientific-literature review; Comparative appraisal of farming practices and innovations

ENSENVI111.name: Dynamic Earth
ENSENVI111.description2: Introduces Earth Science by focusing on interactions among the deep earth, lithosphere and hydrosphere. Highlights key cycles shaping Earth’s surface and includes indoor/outdoor labs and a multi‑day field excursion.
ENSENVI111.profile: Introduces Earth science by linking surface geology to deep-Earth and geophysical processes. Students study rocks, minerals, sedimentation, deformation, stratigraphy, plate tectonics, seismology, the mantle and core, and interactions with climate and other Earth systems. Field and practical work teaches observation and measurement, rock and mineral identification, and reconstruction of geological history. An Ardennes field investigation produces a geological cross-section, stratigraphic column and interpretive report.
ENSENVI111.topics: Plate tectonics and the Wilson cycle; Minerals and rock formation; Volcanism and metamorphism; Sedimentation and facies; Structural deformation; Stratigraphy and palaeontology; Seismology and seismic waves; Geomagnetism and gravity; Mantle and core processes; Earth-system and climate interactions; Geological history; Geohazards
ENSENVI111.methods: Geological field observation and measurement; Rock and mineral identification; Geological mapping and profiling; Stratigraphic-column construction; Geological cross-section construction; Sediment and facies interpretation; Geological-history reconstruction

ENSENVI213.name: Earth System Science Tools
ENSENVI213.description2: Explores interactions among biosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and atmosphere. Teaches system modelling, uses proxies and isotope tracers to study past and future climates and includes a field trip focused on greenhouse gas pathways.

ENSENVI311.name: Environmental Biogeochemistry
ENSENVI311.description2: Investigates natural waters and their interactions with rocks, soils and minerals. Examines biogeochemical processes and cycles, including weathering, mineral formation, absorption, water treatment and resource recovery; utilises geochemical modelling and a case study.
ENSENVI311.profile: Examines chemical and biological controls on near-surface Earth systems, especially interactions among water, minerals, rocks and soils. Students study aqueous composition, equilibrium, speciation, carbonate and redox chemistry, adsorption, weathering and biomineralization. Laboratory investigations and geochemical modelling connect these processes to contaminant behaviour, wastewater treatment, remediation and resource recovery. A project applies geochemical principles to a current environmental issue.
ENSENVI311.topics: Natural-water composition; Chemical equilibrium and ionic activity; Aqueous speciation and complexation; Mineral saturation, precipitation and dissolution; Carbonate equilibria, alkalinity and buffering; Ocean acidification; Redox processes and microbial controls; Adsorption and mineral surfaces; Weathering and clay formation; Biomineralization; Contaminant transport; Environmental remediation and resource recovery
ENSENVI311.methods: Geochemical equilibrium and speciation modelling; Geochemist's Workbench; Piper diagrams; Pourbaix and stability diagrams; Laboratory geochemical investigations; Geochemical data interpretation

ENSGATE101.name: Sustainability Essentials I
ENSGATE101.description2: Provides key concepts in physics, chemistry, materials science, mathematics and modelling necessary for sustainability. Uses a case study to connect concepts to real‑world sustainability challenges and prepares students for 200‑level sustainability courses.
ENSGATE101.profile: Uses planetary boundaries to introduce scientific tools for understanding sustainability and human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and learn chemical, thermodynamic and mechanical principles relevant to environmental processes. Topics connect climate, ocean acidification, nutrient cycles, energy and materials. An iterative laboratory project makes starch-based biopolymers and measures their strength and elasticity to improve the formulation.
ENSGATE101.topics: Planetary boundaries and the Anthropocene; Exponential growth and environmental change; Graphs, rates and uncertainty; Dynamic systems; Chemical bonds, reactions and equilibria; Ocean acidification and nutrient cycles; Thermodynamics and entropy; Greenhouse gases and energy; Ozone depletion; Newtonian mechanics, stress and strain; Biopolymers and material properties
ENSGATE101.methods: Graph interpretation and comparison; Fermi estimation; Difference-equation and first-order linear differential-equation modelling; Elementary differentiation and integration; Biopolymer preparation; Strength and elasticity measurement; Iterative experimental improvement

ENSSUST111.name: Climate Change
ENSSUST111.description2: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.
ENSSUST111.profile: Introduces climate-change science, societal impacts, and mitigation and adaptation. Students examine greenhouse gases, feedbacks, tipping points, ocean acidification and sea-level rise, then consequences for ecosystems, agriculture, transport, buildings and health. Climate justice, governance, communication and misinformation connect physical changes to social responses. Solution pathways include energy systems, carbon removal and climate-adaptive planning. Students interview a stakeholder and produce a short film, alongside reflection on their own role.
ENSSUST111.topics: Anthropogenic climate change; Greenhouse gases; Feedback loops and tipping points; Ocean acidification and sea-level rise; Biosphere impacts; Agriculture, transport and construction; Climate and health; Climate justice and governance; Paris Agreement; Renewable energy and sustainable heat; Carbon removal and geoengineering; Climate communication and misinformation; Climate anxiety; Mitigation and adaptation
ENSSUST111.methods: Stakeholder interviewing; Short-film production for climate communication; Source-credibility evaluation; What? So What? Now What? reflective model

ENSSUST313.name: Research in a Sustainable Delta
ENSSUST313.description2: In this project course you will work in small teams of two or three students on a research problem relevant for sustainability in the broadest sense. We are looking for collaborations with local companies and other institutions. The research questions are supplied by a regional institution or company that is active in areas related to sustainability in the broadest sense. In this way it is guaranteed that the research projects are indeed relevant for the Zeeland delta. Furthermore, students will have access to expertise and/or facilities of the external partner, which will broaden their perspective. Usually, there will be one person affiliated with the external partner organization involved with a project team as external advisor
ENSSUST313.profile: Provides a research-project setting for sustainability questions supplied by organizations and companies in the Zeeland delta. Small teams work with an external advisor to review literature, formulate a research question, plan and execute an investigation, and develop a final product, design or report. The substantive topic and practical techniques depend on the partner project; the common focus is an evidence-based research process and engagement with external stakeholders.
ENSSUST313.topics: Regionally situated sustainability problems; Research-question development; Research planning; Academic literature and evidence; External stakeholder collaboration; Applied sustainability investigation

HCBBIOM211.name: Functional Anatomy
HCBBIOM211.description2: Introduces human body functioning using imaging, surface anatomy and dissection materials. Shows how anatomy serves function and discusses ethical considerations of learning from the dead.
HCBBIOM211.profile: Studies human anatomical structure in relation to function through regional and body-system blocks. Skeletal, thoracic, cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, reproductive and lower urinary anatomy are developed through spatial reasoning, medical images, anatomical drawing and human-specimen material. Guided practicals and dissection-room observation connect three-dimensional relationships to variation. Historical, ethical and societal questions about human remains, representation and sex accompany the anatomical study; activities are framed as academic learning rather than clinical qualification.
HCBBIOM211.topics: Anatomical terminology and body planes; Medical imaging; Skeletal system and vertebral column; Thorax and pelvis; Respiratory and cardiovascular systems; Abdominal organs and vascular supply; Reproductive and lower urinary systems; Anatomical variation and intersex presentations; Human remains and dissection ethics; History and representation of the body
HCBBIOM211.methods: Surface-anatomy observation; Anatomical image interpretation; Scientific anatomical drawing; Three-dimensional anatomical reasoning; Guided study of human skeletal remains and anatomical specimens; Ethical reflection on anatomical practice

HCBBIOM311.name: Pharmacology
HCBBIOM311.description2: Covers the science of drugs—their origin, composition, kinetics, therapeutic use and toxicity. Discusses drug targets, interactions and kinetics, enabling students to explain therapies in terms of molecular targets and physiological consequences.
HCBBIOM311.profile: Studies how drugs act at molecular, cellular and whole-body levels and how the body handles them. Pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, metabolism, toxicity and pharmacogenomics provide foundations for rational therapies and drug-target identification. Applications emphasize nervous-system drugs, antimicrobial treatment and inflammatory, immune and airway conditions. Quantitative exercises and virtual experiments model drug responses, while a psychoactive-drug project proposes a testable follow-up experiment.
HCBBIOM311.topics: Drug discovery and targets; Drug-receptor interactions; Pharmacodynamics; Absorption, distribution, metabolism and elimination; Pharmacokinetics; Antimicrobial therapy; Inflammation and immunopharmacology; Autonomic regulation; Neurotransmission and psychoactive drugs; Pharmacogenomics; Drug toxicity; Access to experimental treatments and evidence; Homeopathy
HCBBIOM311.methods: Concentration-response modelling; Pharmacokinetic time-concentration and time-response analysis; Pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic parameter calculation; Virtual organ-bath experiments; Hypothesis and experimental-design development

HCBBIOM312.name: Infection & Immunity
HCBBIOM312.description2: Explores fundamental processes in immunology such as recognition of self vs non‑self, lymphocyte receptor development and innate and adaptive immune responses. Examines host‑pathogen interactions, inflammation, tissue damage and immunopathology.
HCBBIOM312.profile: Examines host-microbe interactions and the immune mechanisms that protect against infection or cause disease. Microbiology and innate defence lead into antibodies, antigen recognition, lymphocyte development and memory, effector responses and mucosal immunity. Vaccination, allergy, immunodeficiency and autoimmunity connect mechanisms to clinical problems. Students analyze lymphocyte phenotypes using original flow-cytometry data and synthesize recent research in an extended and graphical abstract.
HCBBIOM312.topics: Infectious agents and microbial virulence; Host defence and immune evasion; Immune cells, organs and cytokines; Innate immunity and complement; Antibodies and antigen recognition; MHC and lymphocyte receptors; Lymphocyte activation, development and memory; Cell- and antibody-mediated immunity; Mucosal immunity; Vaccination and viral infections; Hypersensitivity and allergy; Immunodeficiency; Autoimmune disease; Outbreak management
HCBBIOM312.methods: Flow-cytometry data analysis and lymphocyte phenotyping; Clinical symptom and mechanism analysis; Medline/PubMed literature searching; Critical analysis of immunological research; Graphical synthesis of scientific findings

HCBBIOM313.name: Mechanisms of Disease
HCBBIOM313.description2: Examines molecular and cellular defects triggering pathologies. Presents clinical cases, discusses disease mechanisms and treatments across systems and includes an assignment to invent an imaginary disease.
HCBBIOM313.profile: Connects normal organ function to pathophysiology across digestive, cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, endocrine and nervous systems. Students integrate anatomy and physiology to explain symptoms, disease mechanisms, diagnostic findings, treatment and prognosis. Published clinical cases develop differential reasoning and appraisal of diagnostic procedures. A creative assignment constructs an imaginary disease whose symptoms, mechanism and proposed treatment must form a coherent pathophysiological account.
HCBBIOM313.topics: Organ-system disease mechanisms; Nutrition and digestive disease; Hematological and cardiovascular disease; Respiratory disease; Renal failure, dialysis and transplantation; Endocrine disorders; Neurological disease; Etiology and pathogenesis; Diagnosis, treatment and prognosis; Medical ethics; Rheumatic disease
HCBBIOM313.methods: Clinical case analysis; Differential diagnosis reasoning; Critical appraisal of diagnostic and laboratory procedures; Integration of anatomy, physiology and clinical evidence; Mechanistic modelling of an imaginary disease; Biomedical literature comparison

HCBCOGN112.name: Neurobiology
HCBCOGN112.description2: Examines evolution and complexity of brains. Explores animal cognition, welfare and research ethics and studies how brain regions and rhythms regulate behaviour through interactive assignments.
HCBCOGN112.profile: Studies nervous systems and behaviour from comparative, evolutionary and physiological perspectives. Brain anatomy and laboratory introductions support analysis of animal behaviour, research models and welfare. The second part connects regulatory behaviour and biological rhythms to sleep, lifestyle drugs, mood and eating disorders. Comparative-anatomy work and a literature-based disorder report apply neurobiological concepts while animal-research assignments examine reduction, refinement and replacement.
HCBCOGN112.topics: Nervous-system evolution and comparative anatomy; Brain cells and morphology; Cerebral circulation and nerves; Animal behaviour and welfare; Sentience and research ethics; Reduction, refinement and replacement; Enrichment and brain development; Regulatory and sexual behaviour; Lifestyle drugs; Circadian rhythms and sleep; Sleeping and eating disorders; Depression and anxiety; Gut-brain axis; Hypothalamus and pineal gland; Dying brain and consciousness
HCBCOGN112.methods: Comparative brain-anatomy analysis; Introductory microscopy and cell staining; Brain-model comparison; Ethical appraisal of animal research and the 3Rs; Literature-based analysis of neurobiological disorders

HCBCOGN212.name: Perception & Action
HCBCOGN212.description2: Explores neural mechanisms behind perception and action. Examines how the brain processes sensory information and guides goal‑directed behaviour using methods from cognitive neuroscience and neuropsychology.

HCBCOGN311.name: Higher Order Functions
HCBCOGN311.description2: Deepens understanding of neurophysiology and neuroanatomy. Explores higher‑level cognitive functions—memory, emotion, social cognition, executive functioning and language—and engages with current research while designing experiments.
HCBCOGN311.profile: Deepens understanding of neuroanatomy, neurophysiology and the experimental study of higher cognitive functions. Students examine attention, memory, emotion, cognitive control, social cognition, pain and consciousness, connecting brain function and dysfunction to behaviour. An attentional-blink experiment provides direct engagement with empirical work. A team research proposal requires literature analysis, a feasible experimental design and ethical reflection, supported by peer review.
HCBCOGN311.topics: Neurotransmission and psychoactive drugs; Brain structure and hemispheric specialization; Attention and attentional blink; Memory and long-term potentiation; Emotion; Cognitive control and executive functions; Social cognition; Pain; Consciousness; Brain-behaviour relationships; Neuroscience research ethics
HCBCOGN311.methods: Cognitive-neuroscience experimental design; Attentional-blink experiment; Critical analysis of scientific literature and empirical data; Research-proposal development; Scientific peer review

HCBGATE101.name: Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine
HCBGATE101.description2: Introduces biochemistry, macromolecules, cells, organ systems, DNA and cell function. Connects fundamentals to health and disease and serves as a starting point for medicine, biomedical science, life science or public health; no lab experience needed.
HCBGATE101.profile: Introduces the molecular and cellular foundations of life and biomedical science. Students study biological molecules, cells and membranes, communication, enzymes and energy metabolism, cell division, DNA and heredity, gene expression, genomes and biotechnology. Scientific experiments and papers are analyzed through short teaching contributions and a research-based mini-symposium. A responsive final component selects additional life- and biomedical-science topics with the class.
HCBGATE101.topics: Biological molecules and chemistry of life; Cells, organelles and membranes; Cellular communication; Enzymes and energy metabolism; Cell cycle and division; DNA and heredity; Gene mutation and molecular medicine; Gene-expression regulation and epigenetics; Genomes; Recombinant DNA and biotechnology
HCBGATE101.methods: Scientific-literature searching and synthesis; Analysis of published biological experiments

HCBGATE102.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior
HCBGATE102.description2: Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.
HCBGATE102.profile: Introduces psychological and neuroscientific explanations of behaviour and mental processes. Students study neural signalling, brain anatomy and development, learning, intelligence, personality, social influence, mental disorders and treatments. Several sessions introduce behavioural, imaging and electrophysiological approaches to neuroscience and their combined use. Interdisciplinary research-article and case analysis connects psychological processes to neural mechanisms and clinical questions.
HCBGATE102.topics: Brain and behaviour; Neural signalling and action potentials; Functional neuroanatomy; Brain development and hemispheric specialization; Associative, non-associative and social learning; Intelligence; Personality and self-concepts; Social influence; Mental disorders and DSM-5-TR; Psychological treatment; Neuroimaging, electrophysiology and converging methods
HCBGATE102.methods: Psychological and neuroscientific research appraisal; Interdisciplinary case-study analysis

HCBLIFE211.name: Molecular Cell Biology
HCBLIFE211.description2: Provides foundation for practical applications in life science. Focuses on cellular biology of eukaryotes and prokaryotes, revisits concepts from introductory courses, examines current research and encourages evaluating reproducibility and modernising methods.
HCBLIFE211.profile: Studies the molecular mechanisms underlying cellular structure, physiology and regulation, primarily in eukaryotes. Bioenergetics, proteins and membranes connect to genome replication, repair and gene expression, followed by trafficking, signalling, division, tissues, stem cells and cancer. Students evaluate research methods and reproducibility and investigate a drug's molecular target, therapeutic action, metabolism and adverse effects through primary literature, a paper and a research poster.
HCBLIFE211.topics: Cellular components and bioenergetics; Proteins and membranes; Cytoskeleton; DNA replication and repair; Genomes; Regulation of gene expression; Membrane transport and trafficking; Cell-signalling pathways; Cell division and fate; Tissue organization; Stem cells; Cancer; Molecular mechanisms of drug action
HCBLIFE211.methods: Critical analysis of primary molecular-biology literature; Evaluation of research-method limitations and reproducibility; Thermodynamic free-energy calculations; Molecular mechanism analysis

HCBLIFE212.name: Human Physiology
HCBLIFE212.description2: Studies normal functioning of the human body, covering structure‑function relationships, energy handling, homeostasis, signalling, organ systems and integration of their functions.
HCBLIFE212.profile: Studies normal function and regulation in the adult human body, linking molecular and cellular processes to integrated organ systems. Homeostasis, signalling and energy handling frame nervous, endocrine, muscular, respiratory, cardiovascular, renal, digestive and reproductive functions. Medical examples illustrate physiological principles. An individual literature-based paper examines a selected physiological or pathophysiological process and is developed through structured peer review and revision.
HCBLIFE212.topics: Cells, tissues and membrane dynamics; Homeostasis and control; Cellular signalling; Endocrine and nervous regulation; Muscles and movement; Breathing and gas exchange; Blood and cardiovascular function; Renal function; Fluid and electrolyte balance; Digestion and metabolism; Growth and exercise physiology; Reproduction and development
HCBLIFE212.methods: Physiological literature review; Medline/PubMed literature searching; Scientific peer review and evidence-based revision

HCBLIFE213.name: Biochemistry
HCBLIFE213.description2: Explores the chemistry of life and biomolecules such as proteins, sugars, lipids and nucleic acids. Discusses metabolic pathways, the role of biomolecules in health and disease and applications in medicine, biotechnology and sustainability.
HCBLIFE213.profile: Examines the chemistry of life, emphasizing biomolecular structure and function, enzymes and metabolic pathways. Students study proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, enzyme kinetics and regulation, glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, the citric-acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation and further carbohydrate, lipid and nitrogen metabolism. Protein-biochemistry techniques are discussed. A literature-based disease project links a biochemical defect to symptoms, diagnostics and treatment, keeping the molecular mechanism central.
HCBLIFE213.topics: Water and weak bonds; Amino acids and protein structure; Protein-biochemistry techniques; Enzyme action, kinetics, regulation and inhibition; Hemoglobin; Carbohydrates and lipids; Metabolic organization; Glycolysis and gluconeogenesis; Citric-acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation; Glycogen and pentose-phosphate metabolism; Fatty-acid and lipid metabolism; Nitrogen and urea cycle; Biochemical mechanisms of disease
HCBLIFE213.methods: Biochemical pathway and disease-mechanism analysis; Primary-literature review

HCBLIFE214.name: Life Science Laboratory
HCBLIFE214.description2: Introduces biochemical and molecular laboratory work. Covers themes like blood, proteins, bacteria, DNA and bioinformatics and provides a foundation for clinical and biomedical research.
HCBLIFE214.profile: Provides hands-on training in biochemical, microbiological and molecular laboratory methods. Blood analysis, microbial culture and hygiene lead into bacterial transformation, green fluorescent protein production and purification, DNA isolation and analysis, and introductory bioinformatics. Students follow and sometimes adapt protocols, interpret experimental results, maintain reproducible laboratory records and communicate findings in scientific reports and figures.
HCBLIFE214.topics: Blood cells and proteins; Blood groups and hemograms; Aseptic culture and bacterial identification; Disinfection and sterilization; Antibiotic susceptibility; Genetically modified bacteria; GFP production and purification; DNA and plasmid analysis; PCR and restriction digestion; Protein and DNA databases; Genotype and population-genetic interpretation; Experimental reproducibility
HCBLIFE214.methods: Pipetting and workflow planning; Microscopy and blood-smear examination; Blood cell counting and hemogram measurement; ELISA; Aseptic culture and purity streaking; Bacterial identification and inhibition-zone testing; Sterilization and disinfection testing; pGLO bacterial transformation; Protein extraction and chromatographic purification; SDS-PAGE; DNA and plasmid isolation; PCR; Restriction digestion and agarose-gel electrophoresis; DNA and protein database searching; Laboratory notebook and scientific-report preparation

HCBLIFE311.name: Molecular Pathology & Genetics
HCBLIFE311.description2: Covers general and molecular pathology and genetics. Studies cell injury, death, inflammation, immunity, tissue repair, regeneration, fibrosis and neoplasia, examines genetic mutations and diseases, and discusses genetic testing and ethical considerations.
HCBLIFE311.profile: Connects cellular pathology with the genetic mechanisms of human disease. Students examine injury and death, inflammation and repair, neoplasia and lymphoid malignancies, then inheritance, genetic variation, epigenetics, molecular diagnosis and genetic treatment. Ethical, legal and safety questions accompany genetic technologies. A two-year research-grant proposal integrates literature, hypotheses, method selection, controls, feasibility and budgeting; an ethics debate examines stakeholder positions.
HCBLIFE311.topics: Cell injury, adaptation and death; Acute and chronic inflammation; Regeneration, repair and fibrosis; Neoplasia; Pulmonary pathology; Leukemia and lymphoma; Genes, genomes and inheritance; Genetic variation and chromosome abnormalities; Gene regulation and epigenetics; Genotype-phenotype relationships; Genetic testing and DNA technologies; Gene-based therapies and cell manipulation; Genetics ethics, law and biosafety
HCBLIFE311.methods: Biomedical literature review; Research-grant proposal design; Hypothesis formulation and experimental-control selection; Research feasibility, timeline and budget planning; Stakeholder-based ethical argument analysis

HCBPSYC313.name: Advanced Research Methods & Statistics
HCBPSYC313.description2: This course guides you through combining results from multiple studies using systematic reviews and meta-analysis a method now essential in psychology, medicine, social science and other disciplines. Want to know what really works? Gain hands-on skills in research synthesis that inform evidence-based policy and practice. You’ll search literature, manage data, and present findings that matter. Learn to calculate effect sizes, synthesize results and assess bias using R.
HCBPSYC313.profile: Teaches systematic review and meta-analysis for synthesizing evidence in medical, behavioural and related research. Students define review questions, search and select studies, extract and code findings, assess bias and compute effect sizes. Hands-on R work fits fixed- and random-effects models, examines heterogeneity and moderators, conducts meta-regression and investigates publication bias. A group project completes a small meta-analysis and presents its methods and results in a research poster.
HCBPSYC313.topics: Systematic-review purpose and limitations; Review protocols and scope; Literature searching and inclusion criteria; Data extraction and study coding; Risk of bias; Effect-size types and transformations; Fixed- and random-effects models; Effect heterogeneity; Moderators and subgroup differences; Meta-regression; Publication bias; Research synthesis and reporting
HCBPSYC313.methods: Systematic literature review; Database searching and study screening; Study-data extraction and coding; Critical risk-of-bias appraisal; R programming and data management; Effect-size calculation and conversion; Fixed- and random-effects meta-analysis; Moderator and subgroup analysis; Meta-regression; Publication-bias analysis; Meta-analytic visualization and reporting

ENSGATE201.name: Sustainability Essentials II
ENSGATE201.description2: Builds on Sustainability Essentials I. Applies tools and knowledge to a real‑world sustainability case study and allows students to delve deeper into aspects connected to their field of interest.
ENSGATE201.profile: Connects wave physics, chemistry and materials science to sustainability questions. Students study wave behaviour and observation methods, chemical analysis, microscopic material structure and macroscopic stress and strain. Practical sessions include wave applications and chemistry laboratory work. Reflective inquiries and a final project critically assess sustainability campaigns, identify greenwashing and communicate evidence-based improvements to a public audience.
ENSGATE201.topics: Electromagnetic and mechanical waves; Wave composition and interference; Optical spectroscopy; Electron microscopy; Inorganic and organic chemistry; Chemical testing; Material structure and crystallography; Stress and strain; Sustainable material design; Geological wave applications; Nuclear power and waste; Greenwashing
ENSGATE201.methods: Oscilloscope wave visualization; Optical-spectroscopy interpretation; Fourier wave analysis; Copper dissolution and chemical analysis; Laboratory logbook documentation; Stress-strain analysis; Mohr's-circle application; Evidence-based greenwashing case analysis; Public sustainability-communication design

ENSDELT311.name: R3: Recycling, Recovery, Remediation
ENSDELT311.description2: Examines strategies and technologies towards a circular economy. Explores resource security and stewardship, develops lab skills and inorganic chemistry knowledge, and connects to themes at the Delta Climate Center.
ENSDELT311.profile: Studies resource circularity through solar-panel recycling, metal recovery from electronic waste, and soil remediation using plants and mycelium. Theory and extensive laboratory work connect material composition and separation technologies to resource yields, environmental consequences and recycling constraints. Students develop leaching protocols, analyze metal concentrations and recovery, cultivate fungal networks, and use microscopy to characterize materials and mycelium growth.
ENSDELT311.topics: Circular resource supply; Solar-cell and solar-panel recycling; Delamination and material separation; Electronic waste; Pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy; Precious-metal recovery; Plastic-recycling legislation; Phytoremediation; Mycoremediation; Mycelium-based soil amendments
ENSDELT311.methods: Solar-panel dismantling and physical separation; Chemical leaching; Experimental-protocol design; ICP metal analysis; Electrochemical recovery; Scanning electron microscopy and EDS; Mycelium cultivation and growth characterization; Recovery-yield and resource-potential calculations
